title: A Brake Wired to a Sensor

scenes.tts: This yeast cell lacks a gene called Rad nine. Irradiate it, and it does not pause in G two. It keeps dividing for several generations, and dies. Hold it back with a drug for a few hours, and it repairs the damage. What was the gene for?
scenes.caption: This yeast cell lacks a gene called RAD9. Irradiate it, and it does not pause in G2. It keeps dividing for several generations, and dies. Hold it back with a drug for a few hours, and it repairs the damage. What was the gene for?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD appears at once: one round budding-yeast cell in cross-section filling about 70% of frame height (grey outline, faint grey fill), small tag top-left 'budding yeast, no RAD9'. Yellow chromosomes in the middle; along the bottom edge a cycle track G1 - S - G2 - M with a white marker gliding along it (schematic). Orange radiation arrows strike; orange breaks open in the yellow chromosomes. The marker slides straight through G2 without slowing; the mother grows a bud that pinches off at its neck carrying broken pieces, budding repeats, and mother and buds dim toward grey. Rewind (the buds slide back into the one cell): a red drug clamp drops onto the track at G2 and the marker stops against it, trembling; the orange breaks close to clean yellow (green tick). A gold question mark grows over 'RAD9' on the tag on 'What was the gene for?'.
scenes.narration: This yeast cell lacks a gene called RAD9. Irradiate it, and it does not pause in G2. It keeps dividing for several generations, and dies. Hold it back with a drug for a few hours, and it repairs the damage. What was the gene for?

scenes.visual: Title over the same cell, which keeps breathing (slow 2% scale pulse) with the marker idling at G2: 'A Brake Wired to a Sensor'.

scenes.tts: So repair could still happen. Rad nine was needed for waiting. Ted Weinert and Leland Hartwell found this in nineteen eighty-eight.
scenes.caption: So repair could still happen. RAD9 was needed for waiting. Ted Weinert and Leland Hartwell found this in 1988.
scenes.visual: Same cell, same clamp. The gold question mark on the tag morphs into a red hourglass icon labelled 'needed for waiting'. A name label slides in at the top edge: 'Weinert and Hartwell, 1988'. The red drug clamp on the track pulses once, then lifts; the marker moves on into M now that the chromosomes are yellow and whole.
scenes.narration: So repair could still happen. RAD9 was needed for waiting. Ted Weinert and Leland Hartwell found this in 1988.

scenes.tts: A year later, they named such controls checkpoints. A checkpoint makes one cell cycle event wait for another. Without it, the cell divides on time, not on completion.
scenes.caption: A year later, they named such controls checkpoints. A checkpoint makes one cell-cycle event wait for another. Without it, the cell divides on time, not on completion.
scenes.visual: The marker slides back to G1. Above the chromosomes a 'job' bar appears (outlined, filling slowly with yellow: 'copy and repair DNA'). A red brake block appears on the track just before M, joined to the job bar by a thin red wire: label 'checkpoint'. The marker waits at the block until the bar fills and turns green, then the block lifts and the marker passes. Replay with the wire snipped (red wire fades out): the marker passes the M line at a fixed tick while the bar is only half full; label 'on time, not on completion'.
scenes.narration: A year later, they named such controls checkpoints. A checkpoint makes one cell-cycle event wait for another. Without it, the cell divides on time, not on completion.

scenes.tts: Now run the logic the other way. What result would have said Rad nine is a repair gene after all?
scenes.caption: Now run the logic the other way. What result would have said RAD9 is a repair gene after all?
scenes.visual: The tag returns to 'no RAD9, irradiated'. The red drug clamp drops back onto the track at G2 and the marker stops against it. Orange breaks reopen in the chromosomes. A gold question card slides in at upper right: 'What result would mean a repair gene?'
scenes.narration: Now run the logic the other way. What result would have said RAD9 is a repair gene after all?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. Question card stays on screen. The held cell breathes slowly; the orange breaks flicker gently; the marker trembles against the clamp. Nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: If the held cells had still failed to repair, that would point to repair, though not prove it. But more time rescued them.
scenes.visual: Split the held cell's future into two faint ghost copies, one above the other: in the upper ghost the breaks stay orange under the clamp (label 'no rescue: points to repair'); in the lower ghost the breaks close to yellow (label 'rescue: waiting'). The upper ghost fades; the lower one becomes the real cell again with a green tick. The question card shrinks away.
scenes.narration: If the held cells had still failed to repair, that would point to repair, though not prove it. But more time rescued them.

scenes.tts: First, the sensor. Broken D N A ends call in a kinase, A T M. Single strands at a stalled replication fork call in A T R. A T M mainly switches on Check two, and A T R, Check one.
scenes.caption: First, the sensor. Broken DNA ends call in a kinase, ATM. Single strands at a stalled replication fork call in ATR. ATM mainly switches on Chk2, and ATR, Chk1.
scenes.visual: Tag changes to 'a vertebrate cell (schematic)'; the cell outline eases from round to a slightly larger oval in the same place. Zoom gently into the chromosomes. One chromosome gets an orange break: a small grey shape 'MRN' binds the broken ends, recruits a red shape 'ATM', and ATM lights up. On a second chromosome a fork opens; a single strand is coated by small grey beads 'RPA', and a red shape 'ATR-ATRIP' docks; a small grey 'TopBP1' touches it and only then does ATR light up. These lit assemblies are the SENSOR for the rest of the film (a red glow at the trouble spot). Zoom back out: ATM tags a separate small red 'Chk2' with a gold phosphate, ATR tags a separate small red 'Chk1', and both lit messengers start along a red wire that draws itself toward the upper right of the cell, where the ENGINE sits: a pink shape 'cyclin B' bound to a white-outlined shape 'Cdk1'. The marker sits in G2.
scenes.narration: First, the sensor. Broken DNA ends call in a kinase, ATM. Single strands at a stalled replication fork call in ATR. ATM mainly switches on Chk2, and ATR, Chk1.

scenes.tts: In G two, these messengers inhibit the C D C twenty-five phosphatases. So C D K one keeps its inhibitory phosphates and stays off. The cell waits.
scenes.caption: In G2, these messengers inhibit the Cdc25 phosphatases. So Cdk1 keeps its inhibitory phosphates and stays off. The cell waits.
scenes.visual: At the engine: two gold phosphate badges sit on Cdk1. A green shape 'Cdc25' approaches to pluck them off; Chk1 and Chk2 arrive along the red wire, put a small gold phosphate tag on Cdc25 and leave; the tagged Cdc25 greys and drifts back. The gold badges stay; Cdk1 stays dim. A red brake block appears on the track at G2 and the marker stops against it, trembling.
scenes.narration: In G2, these messengers inhibit the Cdc25 phosphatases. So Cdk1 keeps its inhibitory phosphates and stays off. The cell waits.

scenes.tts: In this branch, nothing was destroyed; the brake is a shift in a phosphate balance. Once the signal is silenced, a cell able to recover moves on.
scenes.visual: The orange break closes to yellow and the stalled fork restarts and finishes copying; only then do ATM and ATR fade from the trouble spots; the red wire dims from the sensor end toward the engine. Chk1 and Chk2 dim; a small grey phosphatase removes the gold tag from Cdc25, which brightens to green and plucks the gold badges off Cdk1. Cdk1 lights up with its pink cyclin B. The red block on the track lifts and the marker moves into M.
scenes.narration: In this branch, nothing was destroyed; the brake is a shift in a phosphate balance. Once the signal is silenced, a cell able to recover moves on.

scenes.tts: Here is the whole idea. A checkpoint is a brake wired to a sensor. While the sensor sees an unfinished job, the brake holds back the next transition. When the cell finally moves, the move is hard to undo.
scenes.visual: Pull back so the whole world is visible and simplified: the sensor glow (red) at the chromosomes, the red wire, the red brake on the engine, the track below. The wire glows bright red while a small orange 'unfinished job' mark sits at the sensor; the mark turns green, the wire fades, the brake swings open, the marker passes into the next stage, and a one-way chevron closes behind it on the track. Big text, centred above the cell for this scene only: 'A brake wired to a sensor'.
scenes.narration: Here is the whole idea. A checkpoint is a brake wired to a sensor. While the sensor sees an unfinished job, the brake holds back the next transition. When the cell finally moves, the move is hard to undo.

scenes.tts: The same wiring guards anaphase. Each pair of sister chromatids should attach to opposite spindle poles, through structures called kinetochores.
scenes.visual: Tag changes to 'PtK1 cell, rat-kangaroo (schematic)'. The cell outline flattens into a wide ellipse in the same place; two grey spindle poles appear left and right; grey microtubules grow out. The yellow chromosomes are shown as the sister-chromatid pairs already copied in S phase; they slide to the middle line, each sister with a small white dot at its centromere (kinetochores) caught by microtubules from opposite poles. The marker sits at M, short of a new mark 'anaphase'. The engine at upper right now shows a blue shape 'APC/C' with a teal 'Cdc20' attached, beside the pink cyclin B-Cdk1, and a purple 'securin'.
scenes.narration: The same wiring guards anaphase. Each pair of sister chromatids should attach to opposite spindle poles, through structures called kinetochores.

scenes.tts: In flat rat-kangaroo cells, Conly Rieder's group found one chromosome attached to only one pole. They destroyed its unattached kinetochore with a laser. Does anaphase still wait?
scenes.visual: One pair sits near the left pole, attached on one side only; its free white kinetochore glows with a pulsing red ring (the SENSOR again) and a red wire runs from it to the blue APC/C. All other pairs are lined up at the middle. A white laser line slices in from the upper left and the unattached kinetochore vanishes with a flash. A gold question card slides in: 'Does anaphase wait?'
scenes.narration: In flat rat-kangaroo cells, Conly Rieder's group found one chromosome attached to only one pole. They destroyed its unattached kinetochore with a laser. Does anaphase still wait?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. Question card stays. Microtubules shimmer slightly; the stranded pair near the left pole drifts a hair; the red wire hangs dim, unplugged at the sensor end. Nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: No. Anaphase followed about twenty minutes later, though that chromosome never reached the middle. The wait signal came from the unattached kinetochore.
scenes.visual: A small clock on the track ticks to 'about 20 min'. The red wire fades out completely. The sisters of every lined-up pair pull apart toward the poles, while the operated chromosome stays near the left pole, never having reached the middle line and never splitting normally between poles (label 'never aligned'). The marker passes 'anaphase'. Then rewind to just before the laser: the pairs snap back to the middle, and the stranded pair near the left pole returns with its red-ringed kinetochore and live red wire.
scenes.narration: No. Anaphase followed about twenty minutes later, though that chromosome never reached the middle. The wait signal came from the unattached kinetochore.

scenes.tts: Unattached kinetochores promote assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex. It holds back the A P C, or anaphase-promoting complex, a ligase that marks proteins for destruction.
scenes.caption: Unattached kinetochores promote assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex. It holds back the APC/C, or anaphase-promoting complex, a ligase that marks proteins for destruction.
scenes.visual: From the red-ringed kinetochore, small red bundles labelled 'MCC' bud off and drift along the red wire to the engine. The blue APC/C with its teal Cdc20 sits at upper right; purple securin and pink cyclin B wait beside it.
scenes.narration: Unattached kinetochores promote assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex. It holds back the APC/C, or anaphase-promoting complex, a ligase that marks proteins for destruction.

scenes.tts: The complex is a decoy key. It fills the slots on C D C twenty that would grip a real target. Securin and cyclin B are kept out.
scenes.caption: The complex is a decoy key. It fills the slots on Cdc20 that would grip a real target. Securin and cyclin B are kept out.
scenes.visual: Close on the APC/C (the rest of the cell stays visible, small, at the edges): teal Cdc20 shows two notches (slots). A red MCC bundle pushes red key-shaped tabs into both notches. Purple securin and pink cyclin B try to dock, bump off the filled notches, and drift back.
scenes.narration: The complex is a decoy key. It fills the slots on Cdc20 that would grip a real target. Securin and cyclin B are kept out.

scenes.tts: When the last kinetochore attaches, the decoys stop coming and come apart. Then the A P C tags securin and cyclin B, and the proteasome destroys them.
scenes.caption: When the last kinetochore attaches, the decoys stop coming and come apart. Then the APC/C tags securin and cyclin B, and the proteasome destroys them.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole cell. The stranded pair's free kinetochore catches a microtubule from the right pole; its red ring goes out and the pair slides to the middle line. The red wire fades from the kinetochore end. At the APC/C the red key tabs fall out of Cdc20's notches and break apart. Purple securin and pink cyclin B dock, gain a chain of small gold ubiquitin tags, travel into a grey barrel 'proteasome', and come out as fragments that fade.
scenes.narration: When the last kinetochore attaches, the decoys stop coming and come apart. Then the APC/C tags securin and cyclin B, and the proteasome destroys them.

scenes.tts: Securin had held separase, a protease, inactive; in vertebrates, so had C D K one. Freed separase cuts the cohesin holding sister chromatids together, and anaphase begins. Losing cyclin B is a major way C D K one turns off.
scenes.caption: Securin had held separase, a protease, inactive; in vertebrates, so had Cdk1. Freed separase cuts the cohesin holding sister chromatids together, and anaphase begins. Losing cyclin B is a major way Cdk1 turns off.
scenes.visual: Purple securin vanishes and Cdk1 dims as its pink cyclin B goes; only with both brakes gone is an orange shape 'separase' released. It moves to the chromosomes and snips the grey cohesin links between each sister pair. The sisters pull to opposite poles; the marker passes 'anaphase' and a one-way chevron closes behind it.
scenes.narration: Securin had held separase, a protease, inactive; in vertebrates, so had Cdk1. Freed separase cuts the cohesin holding sister chromatids together, and anaphase begins. Losing cyclin B is a major way Cdk1 turns off.

scenes.tts: Why does it not run backwards? A phosphate can be put back within seconds to minutes, because the protein is still there. A destroyed protein must be made again.
scenes.visual: The engine area splits into two small side-by-side panels inside the cell. Left: a gold phosphate badge pops off a protein and pops back on, twice (label 'seconds to minutes'). Right: a purple securin breaks into fragments that fade; its outline stays dashed and empty (label 'must be made again'). The separated sisters stay at the poles behind them.
scenes.narration: Why does it not run backwards? A phosphate can be put back within seconds to minutes, because the protein is still there. A destroyed protein must be made again.

scenes.tts: Potapova and colleagues forced cells out of mitosis with a C D K one inhibitor. Cyclin B was kept. After washout, many went back into mitosis. Cells whose cyclin B was destroyed did not.
scenes.caption: Potapova and colleagues forced cells out of mitosis with a Cdk1 inhibitor. Cyclin B was kept. After washout, many went back into mitosis. Cells whose cyclin B was destroyed did not.
scenes.visual: Back in the one cell, rewound to mitosis. A grey drug cap lands on Cdk1 (pink cyclin B still bound); the marker leaves M forward onto a short side branch labelled 'G1-like state'. The cap lifts away: Cdk1 lights up again and the marker slides from the side branch back into M (label 'cyclin B kept: returns'). Replay with cyclin B shattered into fragments before the cap lifts: Cdk1 stays dim and the marker stays out (label 'cyclin B destroyed: stays out').
scenes.narration: Potapova and colleagues forced cells out of mitosis with a Cdk1 inhibitor. Cyclin B was kept. After washout, many went back into mitosis. Cells whose cyclin B was destroyed did not.

scenes.tts: Entry into mitosis also rests on feedback. Active C D K one switches on its activator and switches off its inhibitor. Once the rise starts, it feeds itself.
scenes.caption: Entry into mitosis also rests on feedback. Active Cdk1 switches on its activator and switches off its inhibitor. Once the rise starts, it feeds itself.
scenes.visual: Rewind the track to late G2. At the engine: green 'Cdc25' and a red shape 'Wee1' sit either side of Cdk1. As Cdk1 brightens a little, a curved green arrow loops from Cdk1 to Cdc25 (Cdc25 brightens) and a blunt red bar from Cdk1 to Wee1 (Wee1 dims). Each loop speeds the next: Cdk1 snaps to full brightness. A small gauge beside the engine, 'Cdk1 activity (schematic)', jumps from low to high.
scenes.narration: Entry into mitosis also rests on feedback. Active Cdk1 switches on its activator and switches off its inhibitor. Once the rise starts, it feeds itself.

scenes.tts: Once on, this switch tends to stay on. That may be why the damage brake normally acts in G two, before the switch flips.
scenes.caption: Once on, this switch tends to stay on. That may be why the damage brake normally acts in G2, before the switch flips.
scenes.visual: The schematic gauge holds high while a red Chk1 arrives along the old red wire and dims Cdc25: the gauge wobbles but stays high (label 'on resists small changes'). Rewind to G2 with the gauge low: the same red Chk1 dims Cdc25 and the gauge stays low (label 'off resists small changes'). The red brake block settles on the track at G2, before the M mark.
scenes.narration: Once on, this switch tends to stay on. That may be why the damage brake normally acts in G2, before the switch flips.

scenes.tts: The brake can leak, though. A cell held in mitosis can eventually slip out, because cyclin B is still slowly destroyed.
scenes.visual: Back to the mitotic cell with one red-ringed unattached kinetochore and the red wire live. Whole pink cyclin B molecules trickle, one at a time, into the grey proteasome and leave as fragments, even with the brake on; Cdk1 slowly dims. The marker slides off M onto a side branch labelled 'slippage: no normal anaphase (schematic)'; the sister pairs stay unseparated.
scenes.narration: The brake can leak, though. A cell held in mitosis can eventually slip out, because cyclin B is still slowly destroyed.

scenes.tts: So at each guarded step, a cell asks one question: is the job finished? Until it is, a sensor holds the brake. Then destruction or feedback carries it forward, and the step is hard to take back.
scenes.visual: The whole world, pulled back and calm: the cell, the sensor spot, the red wire, the engine, the track. One last time, in quick summary: the sensor glows red and the brake holds the marker; the sensor goes green, the brake lifts, securin and cyclin B fragment at the engine and the Cdk1 gauge falls, and the marker passes with a one-way chevron closing behind it. Everything settles; slow ambient breathing continues.
scenes.narration: So at each guarded step, a cell asks one question: is the job finished? Until it is, a sensor holds the brake. Then destruction or feedback carries it forward, and the step is hard to take back.

scenes.visual: End card
scenes.line: Checkpoints make the cell wait; destruction and feedback make it commit.
